items.passage:
Read the conversation between two university classmates.

Ploy: Have you heard from Krit? Our slides are due on Monday and he still hasn't sent his section.
Ben: Not a word. I messaged him twice yesterday. (1) ______
Ploy: Maybe something's happened. He's usually pretty reliable.
Ben: True. I'd hate to accuse him of slacking off if he's actually ill or something.
Ploy: (2) ______ Why don't you call him instead of sending another message? A call is harder to ignore.
Ben: Fair enough. But if we still haven't heard anything by tomorrow, (3) ______
Ploy: Agreed. We can split his part between us and explain the situation to Dr Anong. She'd rather know now than find out halfway through the presentation.
items.stem: Which choice best completes gap (1)?
choices: He replied straight away, actually.
He's seen them, but he hasn't replied.
I'm going to tell Dr Anong he's lazy.
He told me he finished it last week.

explanation.en: Ben has had 'not a word' from Krit, so 'He's seen them, but he hasn't replied.' fits. Replying or saying he has finished contradicts 'Not a word', and calling him lazy conflicts with Ben's later wish not to accuse him unfairly.
explanation.th: เบนไม่ได้รับคำตอบเลย ('Not a word') จึงต้องเป็น 'He's seen them, but he hasn't replied.' (อ่านแล้วแต่ไม่ตอบ) การตอบกลับทันทีหรือบอกว่าทำเสร็จแล้วขัดกับ 'Not a word' และการกล่าวหาว่าขี้เกียจขัดกับที่เบนไม่อยากกล่าวหาเพื่อนโดยไม่เป็นธรรม

Read the conversation at a hotel reception desk.

Receptionist: Good evening, welcome to the Riverside Hotel. Are you checking in?
Guest: Yes, the name's Morgan. I booked a double room with a river view for three nights.
Receptionist: Let me see... Ah. I'm very sorry, Mr Morgan. (9) ______ We've had a problem with the air conditioning in all the river-view rooms on that floor.
Guest: You're joking. I chose this hotel specifically for the view. It's our anniversary.
Receptionist: I completely understand, and I do apologise. (10) ______ Alternatively, I can give you a city-view room tonight and move you to a river-view room tomorrow, with dinner in our restaurant on us this evening.
Guest: What exactly would the first option involve?
Receptionist: A suite at our sister hotel, five minutes away, at no extra cost. It's also on the river.

Receptionist: Of course. I'll make a note to move you first thing tomorrow.
items.stem: Which choice best completes gap (9)?
choices: Your room has been upgraded to a suite here.
You'll have to pay extra for the view, I'm afraid.
It seems your river-view room isn't available tonight.
The hotel is fully booked for the next three nights.

explanation.en: The receptionist apologises and blames the air conditioning in the river-view rooms, so the problem is 'It seems your river-view room isn't available tonight.' An upgrade would not need an apology, and a fully booked hotel contradicts the offer of a city-view room.

items.passage:
Read the interview between Fah, a student journalist, and Mr Hughes, the university's sustainability officer.

Fah: Thanks for making time for this, Mr Hughes. Our readers have been asking about the new food-waste scheme in the canteens. Could you start by explaining what's changed?
Mr Hughes: Certainly. Since January, every canteen vendor has weighed the food that's thrown away at the end of each day. (13) ______ — we simply had no idea how much was being wasted.
Fah: And what did the figures show?
Mr Hughes: Roughly 400 kilograms a day across the campus. About a third of that was unsold cooked food; the rest was what students left on their plates.
Fah: That's a lot. Students have complained that portions got smaller this term. Is that connected?
Mr Hughes: (14) ______ Vendors can now offer half portions at a lower price. Full portions are the same size as before. But I take the point — we didn't communicate the change very well.
Fah: What happens to the waste now?
Mr Hughes: Unsold food that's still safe goes to a local charity kitchen every evening. Plate waste goes to the composting unit behind the Faculty of Agriculture, and the compost is used in the university gardens.
Fah: Some people say composting is just a way of making waste look green. (15) ______
Mr Hughes: There's some truth in that. Composting is better than landfill, but the best food waste is the waste we never create. That's why the half-portion option matters more, in my view, than the composting.
Fah: Has the scheme actually reduced waste?
Mr Hughes: It's early days. Plate waste is down about fifteen per cent, but unsold food has barely changed. (16) ______
Fah: So what's next?

Lingora Plus — is the premium plan worth it? ★★★☆☆ reviewed by Thanawat S.

I've been using the free version of Lingora for about a year to keep up my Japanese, and last month I finally gave in and paid for Lingora Plus (1,290 baht a year). Here's what changed — and what didn't.

The headline feature is the AI conversation partner, and it is genuinely clever. It adapts to your level, corrects mistakes gently and lets you practise situations like ordering food or asking for directions. My only complaint is that it is a little too patient: in a month of chatting, it has never once failed to understand me, which is more than I can say for real people in Osaka.

Removing adverts makes the app feel calmer, and offline lessons are handy on the BTS. But the much-advertised "personalised review" feature is a disappointment. It simply repeats the words I got wrong most recently, which the free version already did, just less attractively.

The bigger problem is that Plus doesn't fix Lingora's weaknesses. Grammar explanations are still thin — a single sentence where a short paragraph is needed — and there is still almost no listening practice at natural speed. If you're aiming for an exam such as the JLPT, you'll need other materials anyway.

So, is it worth it? If you enjoy the app and want to speak more, the conversation partner alone justifies the price. If you were hoping Plus would turn Lingora into a complete course, save your money.

items.passage:
University sets rules for AI in coursework

BANGKOK — A leading Thai university will require students to declare any use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in their coursework from next semester, under a policy approved by its academic senate on Wednesday.

The policy stops short of a ban. Instead, each course will be placed by its lecturer in one of three categories: courses in which AI tools are not permitted, courses in which they may be used for limited tasks such as brainstorming or checking grammar, and courses in which they may be used freely as long as their use is declared. Students who fail to declare their use of AI will be treated as having committed academic misconduct.

"Banning these tools outright would be both unenforceable and short-sighted," said Associate Professor Rattana Phongsri, the vice-president for academic affairs. "Our graduates will use AI in their careers. The question is not whether they use it, but whether they use it honestly and well."

The university will also change how some work is assessed. Take-home essays in first-year courses will be partly replaced by in-class writing and short oral examinations, in which students explain and defend the work they have submitted.

Reaction among students has been broadly positive, though some have raised concerns about consistency. "If one lecturer allows AI and another doesn't, for very similar assignments, that's confusing," said Pakorn, a third-year law student. "We need clear examples, not just categories."

Some lecturers, meanwhile, question whether declarations will be truthful. Detection software, they note, is unreliable and has wrongly flagged work by students writing in a second language. The university says it will not use such software as the sole evidence of misconduct.

A review of the policy is scheduled for the end of the academic year.
items.stem: What is the main topic of the report?
choices: A university's decision to ban AI tools completely
Students' complaints about unreliable detection software
A university's new rules allowing AI in coursework under certain conditions
A plan to replace all essays with oral examinations

explanation.en: The report explains a policy that 'stops short of a ban' and sets categories and declaration rules — new rules allowing AI in coursework under certain conditions. Detection software and oral exams are supporting details.
explanation.th: ข่าวอธิบายนโยบายที่ 'stops short of a ban' โดยแบ่งประเภทรายวิชาและกำหนดให้แจ้งการใช้ AI จึงเป็นกฎใหม่ที่อนุญาตให้ใช้ AI ภายใต้เงื่อนไข ส่วนซอฟต์แวร์ตรวจจับและการสอบปากเปล่าเป็นรายละเอียดประกอบ

items.passage:
The myth of multitasking

Watch a university student at work and you are likely to see several things happening at once: a lecture recording playing at double speed, a group chat flashing in the corner of the screen, a phone face-up on the desk. Many young people describe themselves as skilled multitaskers, and in a world of constant notifications it can seem like a necessary skill. The research, however, tells a less flattering story.

Strictly speaking, the human brain cannot give full attention to two demanding tasks at the same time. What feels like multitasking is usually rapid switching: attention moves from the essay to the message and back again. Each switch carries a cost. The brain has to drop the "rules" of one task and load those of the next, and this takes time — often only a fraction of a second, but enough to add up over an evening. More seriously, after an interruption people frequently take several minutes to return to the depth of concentration they had before.

Switching also seems to affect the quality of what we produce. In laboratory studies, participants who are interrupted while writing tend to make more errors and produce work that is judged less thoughtful than that of participants who work without interruption, even when the total time spent is the same. Ironically, those who multitask most often are not necessarily better at it. Some studies have found that heavy media multitaskers perform worse on tests of filtering out irrelevant information, although researchers disagree about whether multitasking causes this weakness or whether people who are easily distracted are simply drawn to multitasking.

There are exceptions. When one of the tasks is automatic — walking while talking, or folding laundry while listening to a podcast — doing both at once causes little difficulty, because the automatic task makes few demands on conscious attention. Problems arise when both tasks require thought, or when the "easy" task turns out to need more attention than expected, as drivers who use their phones discover.

If multitasking is so inefficient, why is it so tempting? Part of the answer is that switching is rewarding in the short term. A new message offers a small, immediate reward, while an essay offers only distant and uncertain ones. Every check of the phone feels like activity, even when little has been accomplished. People also tend to overestimate their own ability: in surveys, those who multitask most are often the most confident that it does them no harm.

The solution is not to retreat from technology but to manage it deliberately. Many students find it helpful to work in focused blocks of 25 to 50 minutes with notifications switched off, followed by short breaks in which they can check messages freely. Others simply put their phones in another room. Such strategies may feel restrictive at first, but they protect what is, for most students, the scarcest resource of all: not time, but undivided attention.

explanation.en: The article argues that multitasking is really 'rapid switching' with costs in time and quality, and recommends managing technology — not banning it. Exceptions apply only to automatic tasks.

items.passage:
The myth of multitasking

Watch a university student at work and you are likely to see several things happening at once: a lecture recording playing at double speed, a group chat flashing in the corner of the screen, a phone face-up on the desk. Many young people describe themselves as skilled multitaskers, and in a world of constant notifications it can seem like a necessary skill. The research, however, tells a less flattering story.

Strictly speaking, the human brain cannot give full attention to two demanding tasks at the same time. What feels like multitasking is usually rapid switching: attention moves from the essay to the message and back again. Each switch carries a cost. The brain has to drop the "rules" of one task and load those of the next, and this takes time — often only a fraction of a second, but enough to add up over an evening. More seriously, after an interruption people frequently take several minutes to return to the depth of concentration they had before.

Switching also seems to affect the quality of what we produce. In laboratory studies, participants who are interrupted while writing tend to make more errors and produce work that is judged less thoughtful than that of participants who work without interruption, even when the total time spent is the same. Ironically, those who multitask most often are not necessarily better at it. Some studies have found that heavy media multitaskers perform worse on tests of filtering out irrelevant information, although researchers disagree about whether multitasking causes this weakness or whether people who are easily distracted are simply drawn to multitasking.

There are exceptions. When one of the tasks is automatic — walking while talking, or folding laundry while listening to a podcast — doing both at once causes little difficulty, because the automatic task makes few demands on conscious attention. Problems arise when both tasks require thought, or when the "easy" task turns out to need more attention than expected, as drivers who use their phones discover.

If multitasking is so inefficient, why is it so tempting? Part of the answer is that switching is rewarding in the short term. A new message offers a small, immediate reward, while an essay offers only distant and uncertain ones. Every check of the phone feels like activity, even when little has been accomplished. People also tend to overestimate their own ability: in surveys, those who multitask most are often the most confident that it does them no harm.

The solution is not to retreat from technology but to manage it deliberately. Many students find it helpful to work in focused blocks of 25 to 50 minutes with notifications switched off, followed by short breaks in which they can check messages freely. Others simply put their phones in another room. Such strategies may feel restrictive at first, but they protect what is, for most students, the scarcest resource of all: not time, but undivided attention.

items.passage:
Science without a laboratory

Every December, thousands of volunteers in dozens of countries spend a day counting birds. They are not professional scientists; many are retired teachers, office workers or schoolchildren with a pair of binoculars and a notebook. Yet the data they collect, gathered over more than a century in some places, has become one of the most valuable records of how bird populations respond to changes in climate and land use. Projects like this are known as citizen science: research in which members of the public help to collect or analyse data.

The idea is not new — amateur naturalists and astronomers made important contributions long before science became a profession — but the internet and smartphones have transformed its scale. Today, volunteers classify images of distant galaxies, transcribe handwritten weather records from old ships' logbooks, and photograph insects in their gardens for apps that identify species automatically. Some projects attract hundreds of thousands of participants.

For scientists, the attractions are obvious. Many research questions require more observations than any team could gather on its own, especially when the data must be collected across large areas or over long periods. Volunteers can be almost everywhere at once, at very little cost. In some cases, humans still outperform computers: people are remarkably good at spotting unusual patterns, and several unexpected discoveries have been made by volunteers who noticed something that automated systems had ignored.

Critics have raised two main concerns. The first is data quality. Volunteers may misidentify species, record observations carelessly, or report only what they find interesting, so that common species are under-recorded. Researchers have responded by building checks into their projects: asking several volunteers to classify the same image, for example, or using statistical methods to correct for the fact that observers visit some places far more than others. Studies comparing volunteer and professional data generally find that, with such checks in place, the differences are smaller than feared.

The second concern is more ethical than technical. If volunteers do much of the work, should they share in the credit? Some projects now list contributors in published papers or name discoveries after the people who made them. Others argue that the relationship should run in both directions, with communities helping to decide which questions are worth asking rather than merely supplying data for questions chosen by professionals. This matters particularly when research concerns local issues such as water pollution, where residents may have knowledge that outsiders lack.

Citizen science will not replace professional research, and it is not suitable for every question; few volunteers can operate a particle accelerator. But it has already changed what is possible in fields from ecology to astronomy. Perhaps just as importantly, it gives thousands of people direct experience of how science actually works — slowly, collectively and with careful attention to error — at a time when public trust in expertise can no longer be taken for granted.

Studies comparing volunteer and professional data generally find that, with such checks in place, the differences are smaller than feared.

The second concern is more ethical than technical. If volunteers do much of the work, should they share in the credit? Some projects now list contributors in published papers or name discoveries after the people who made them. Others argue that the relationship should run in both directions, with communities helping to decide which questions are worth asking rather than merely supplying data for questions chosen by professionals. This matters particularly when research concerns local issues such as water pollution, where residents may have knowledge that outsiders lack.

Citizen science will not replace professional research, and it is not suitable for every question; few volunteers can operate a particle accelerator. But it has already changed what is possible in fields from ecology to astronomy. Perhaps just as importantly, it gives thousands of people direct experience of how science actually works — slowly, collectively and with careful attention to error — at a time when public trust in expertise can no longer be taken for granted.
items.stem: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards citizen science?
choices: Convinced that it will replace professional research
Mainly concerned about its ethical problems
Doubtful that it produces any useful data
Broadly positive, while recognising its limitations

explanation.en: The writer praises what it has 'already changed' but says it 'will not replace professional research' and 'is not suitable for every question' — broadly positive, while recognising its limitations.

[4] Before a scientific study is published in a journal, it usually goes through a process called peer review.
[5] If the editor considers it suitable, he or she sends it to two or three independent experts in the field.
items.stem: The sentences above are in jumbled order. Which order makes the most logical paragraph?

explanation.en: [4] – [2] – [5] – [1] – [3]: the sentence naming 'peer review' introduces the topic; 'first submit' is step one; 'If the editor considers it suitable' follows submission; 'These reviewers' must come after the experts are mentioned; asking for changes is the final stage.
explanation.th: [4] – [2] – [5] – [1] – [3]: ประโยคที่กล่าวถึง 'peer review' เป็นบทนำ 'first submit' คือขั้นแรก 'If the editor considers it suitable' ตามหลังการส่ง 'These reviewers' ต้องมาหลังการกล่าวถึงผู้เชี่ยวชาญ และการแก้ไขเป็นขั้นสุดท้าย

items.stem: The sentences above are in jumbled order. Which order makes the most logical paragraph?

explanation.th: [5] – [3] – [6] – [1] – [4] – [2]: เริ่มด้วยความคาดหวังของเล็ก คำว่า 'however' แสดงความขัดแย้งกับเช้าวันแรกที่วุ่นวาย ตามด้วยความผิดพลาด 'Fortunately' นำความช่วยเหลือของผู้จัดการ แล้วจึงเป็นพัฒนาการ 'by the end of the week' และปิดด้วยความคิดเห็นในภายหลัง
